schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch survey the whole chapter's shape (the two fighting days, the two rest-days, the birth of Purim); Ellicott glosses 'drew near' as arrived or came, as in Esther 8:17.

Henry frames a decisive open battle in which the enemies were the aggressors, hoping by the former edict to prevail; the Chaldee names them Amalekites, infatuated like Pharaoh, but the day they reckoned theirs proved God's day.
Clarke marvels at the many ordinary providences that saved a doomed people, none too low for God to lift up nor too high to cast down, a hand the heathen must have seen.
Gill fixes the date: the twelfth month, Adar, the thirteenth day, the term appointed by both decrees.

Keil and Delitzsch parse 'in their cities' and the idiom of stretching out the hand to kill (Esther 2:21; 3:6), none standing before them for fear; Ellicott doubts the Jews kept strictly to defence, suspecting they pressed their advantage into vengeance (shown by v.16).
Gill: they gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces, wherever they lived.
Wesley: the enemies, though they took up arms, were easily conquered and destroyed.
Henry: they stood on their defence in concert, and God struck all people with a fear of them, as the Canaanites feared Israel (Josh. 2:9).

debates.question: Did the Jews act in strict self-defence, or press their advantage into vengeance?

sides.position: strict self-defence, standing for their lives only when attacked
a favoured people using their opportunity well past the bounds of mere defence

themes: the fear that fell on all
the second edict repealing the first

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: all the rulers and satraps supported the Jews because the fear of Mordecai fell on them; Ellicott notes 'helped' is literally 'lifted up,' the verb rendered 'furthered' at Ezra 8:36.
Gill lingers on the verb 'blessed'—countenanced, encouraged, extolled, lifted up, as the Targum has it.
Clarke: the officers assisted with their own troops, and it does not appear the Jews slew any who did not rise up to destroy them (cf. v.5).
Henry: they helped not from kindness but from the fear of Mordecai, who had the countenance of God and king; great men may by their influence do much good.
Gill: Mordecai was not only over Esther's affairs but one of the king's counsellors, the chief minister of state.
Keil and Delitzsch: much esteemed, his fame spreading (cf. Joshua 6:27; Jer. 6:24), a participle of one growing continually greater, like Jehoshaphat (2 Chron. 17:12).
Henry: the influence of one good man raised high becomes a shelter for many, since even those who fear not God stand in awe of him whom God has advanced.

themes: one man a wall to a nation

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch parse the verb of smiting (2 Sam. 23:10; Num. 22:6) and read 'did what they would' as retaliation at their discretion, per the decree of Esther 8:11; Ellicott presses the same discretion toward vengeance rather than pure defence.
Gill pictures the weapons—swords, clubs, and staves, as the Targum says.
Clarke reads the discretion narrowly: it does not appear the Jews slew any who did not rise up to destroy them.
Henry: they smote only those found in arms, none of whom escaped.

outliers.note: Reads the leave to do 'according to their will' as an opening toward vengeance rather than pure defence, against the restraint Clarke and Henry find.

themes: the total defeat of the enemies

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'the palace' means the whole royal city, not the palace precincts, where even Xerxes would allow no bloodshed but by direct order; Keil and Delitzsch give the 500 in round numbers and begin their note on the columned writing of Haman's sons' names.
Clarke wonders that 500 could rise where the king's mind was so well known; Wesley: the slain were such as would watch every chance to destroy the Jews.
Gill: the slaughter was in the city, not the palace; these were Haman's enraged faction, headed by his ten sons—princes of Amalek, says the Targum.

themes: the palace as the royal city

schools.summary: Gill reads the ten names through to Vajezatha and sets the sons at the head of the five hundred, the ringleaders of the assault.
Keil and Delitzsch explain the columned writing of the names (meant only for prominence and counting, not the Rabbis' hidden portents) and note the spoil untouched though allowed by Esther 8:11.

themes: at the head of the five hundred
the roll of the enemy's house

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch carry the list forward, the ten set one beneath another to be counted, closing at Vajezatha with his enlarged final letter, and caution against loading the arrangement with hidden meaning.

Henry preserves the custom of reading the ten names in one breath (all slain in one moment, from Buxtorf) and the Chaldee that Zeresh with seventy more of Haman's children fled and begged their bread.

themes: the continued roll of Haman's sons
the ten read in one breath

schools.summary: Clarke: the Jews took no spoil, proof they sought safety not property, though the edict allowed it (Esther 8:11); Wesley: they left the goods to the enemies' children, that it might appear they acted from necessity and self-preservation, not malice or covetousness.
Ellicott notes the liberty foregone—this they might have done, according to the edict.

Henry's threefold honour: contempt of worldly wealth like Abraham with Sodom's spoil; aiming only at preservation; and humanity that spared the women and little ones, leaving them the spoil for subsistence.

themes: on the spoil they laid not their hand

schools.summary: Gill gives two motives for the report: the king's own wish to know his losses, or others' officious design to irritate him against the Jews.
Keil and Delitzsch record the account given to the king and his turning to Esther with a fresh question.
Henry hears in the king's ready telling of the numbers to Esther the tenderness he still bore her.

outliers.note: Leaves the messenger's motive open—the same report an honest reckoning or a malicious whisper, according to the heart that carried it.

themes: the number brought to the king

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: the king, astonished at the 500, infers far more slain in the provinces, then renews his boundless offer as at the sceptre and banquet (Esther 5:6; 7:2).
Gill sets the exchange after the account had been brought in.
Wesley: the king reckons the great slaughter as proof he has fully granted her petition, yet stands ready to grant anything further.

Wesley defends the second day as reaching the worst enemies who had hidden themselves, and the hanging as public infamy and terror; Clarke reads the exposure of the already-slain sons as a warning to any who still sought the Jews' destruction.
Henry clears Esther of cruelty: she was none of the blood-thirsty but had good reasons—the utter crushing of a malignant party, the disgrace of Haman's house.
Gill notes only her submission, 'if it please the king.'

Ellicott charges her with simple blood-thirstiness: the Jews were in no danger, a second day was needless butchery, and hanging the dead sons a gratuitous outrage—though she must not be judged by the high Christian standard.

debates.question: Was Esther's request for a second day and the hanging of Haman's sons justified, or blood-thirsty?

sides.position: a righteous, necessary defence and a just terror to the enemy
needless butchery and a gratuitous outrage on the dead—an indefensible stain

themes: the Old Testament versus the Christian standard

schools.summary: Gill: leave for the Jews to seek and slay their remaining enemies in Shushan on the fourteenth, as on the thirteenth.
Keil and Delitzsch: the decree concerns the leave to fight the next day, not the hanging (cf. Esther 8:13); the hanging of the sons is added only in a trailing clause.
Henry: it was done accordingly, the bodies supposed hung in chains for a time, for public disgrace and lasting terror.

themes: the decree for the second day

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: 300 more slain, the spoil again untouched (cf. v.10); Ellicott mends the opening word to 'and the Jews.'
Gill: they gathered on the fourteenth as on the thirteenth.
Clarke: Mordecai had warned many enemies escaped the first day; 300 more found, 800 in all, and Susa purged of its enemies.

Keil and Delitzsch: the Jews stood for their lives, had rest, slew 75,000, took no spoil, the word of rest set early to show how it ended; Ellicott prefers the LXX's 15,000 and cites Wordsworth on the reckless Eastern despotism and the providence at Salamis.
Gill: they gathered in a body in their several provinces and cities.
Henry: if all were Amalekites, the remembrance of Amalek was now blotted out (Exod. 17:14); the vast execution was justified as necessary defence.

debates.question: How many enemies fell in the provinces?

sides.position: fifteen thousand, as the Septuagint, perhaps the more probable

schools.summary: Gill ties 'the thirteenth day' back to v.16, the day of the provincial slaughter, with rest and feasting on the fourteenth.
Henry: they kept the day of rest, not the day of battle—the pattern of the sabbath—and celebrated at once, for thankful returns should be swift while the mercy is fresh.
Ellicott: both the fourteenth and fifteenth are now kept as Purim, the fourteenth chief; Keil and Delitzsch: Susa fought both days and rested the fifteenth, making it their day of joy.
Clarke: two days employed in slaying their enemies, and rest on the fifteenth.
Gill: the Jews of Shushan fought both the thirteenth and fourteenth, the decree renewed for the second day.
Henry marks the doubling—those in Shushan kept the fifteenth, both days observed, the festival always on the day of rest.

Ellicott: 'villages' and 'unwalled towns' are virtually one Hebrew word, country places undefended by bulwarks (cf. Deut. 3:5); Keil and Delitzsch record the fourteenth made a day of gladness and sending portions.
Gill relays Jarchi's rule: unwalled towns keep the fourteenth, walled towns (from Joshua's day) the fifteenth, Susa the fifteenth for the miracle done in it.
Clarke: the rich sent portions to the poor, that the joy might be as general as the sorrow had been.
Gill: Mordecai wrote the transactions and the letter; some conclude he was the book's penman, though it does not necessarily follow.
Clarke: Mordecai's authorship may extend only thus far, the rest added by Ezra or the Great Synagogue; from here on is recapitulation and the appointing of Purim.
Henry contrasts Mordecai's God-less style with Nehemiah's; because so little of the language of Canaan appears, many think the book drawn from the Persian journals, not written by Mordecai.

debates.question: Did Mordecai write the book of Esther?

sides.position: perhaps, though it does not necessarily follow
his part extends only to here; the rest added by Ezra or the Great Synagogue
likely not—the book drawn from the journals of the kings of Persia

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch give the appointment of the fourteenth and fifteenth yearly, the month turned from sorrow to joy; Ellicott notes Mordecai now adds the fifteenth to the fourteenth the provinces already kept.
Gill: 'to stablish this' is to make a permanent, annually observed thing of what they had done.
Henry marks the season, a month before the passover, and the keeping of two whole days as thanksgiving.
Gill grounds the days in the rest from enemies, all who rose up having been slain.
Keil and Delitzsch lay out the fourfold command: feasting, joy, sending portions, and gifts to the poor.
Henry expounds the three duties—cheerfulness (Eccl. 10:19), generosity, and charity to the poor and maimed (Luke 14:13)—thanksgiving and almsgiving together.
Gill: they kept the days in a civil, not a religious, way—commemorating a benefit, not adding to the law; yet some elders later scrupled it as an innovation.
Keil and Delitzsch: the people confirmed what they had themselves begun, making it an annual custom at Mordecai's writing.
Clarke: they bound themselves, their successors, and proselytes to keep it yearly—kept unbroken in every place of the dispersion to this day.

Keil and Delitzsch: Haman devised destruction and cast Pur, the lot, the verb of ruin being that used of God's own routing of enemies (Exod. 14:24; Deut. 2:15); Ellicott refers Pur back to Esther 3:7.
Gill: Haman had formed a design to exterminate the Jews from the whole empire in one day.

Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott take the subject impersonally—'when it, the matter, came before the king'—since Esther is not named in the context and stands in italics; the device returned on Haman's head, and he and his sons were hanged.
Gill reads it of the queen—'when Esther came before the king' to plead for her life and her people's.

debates.question: Does 'when she/it came before the king' refer to Esther or to the matter?

sides.position: Esther the queen came before the king
impersonal—the matter came before the king (Esther not named)

schools.summary: Wesley and Clarke trace the name to Pur, the lot Haman cast for month and day; the letter recalled as seen is Mordecai's (v.20).

Keil and Delitzsch expound the twofold 'therefore'—the reason for the name, and the two grounds (Mordecai's letter and the people's own experience) of its general keeping; Ellicott notes Purim still kept on the 14th and 15th, the whole book read each year.
Gill: they called the days Purim after Pur, the lot, because of the lots Haman cast.
Henry draws the theology from the name: the God at whose disposal the lot is outwitted the diviners in their own craft (Isa. 44:25).

themes: the lot disposed by the LORD

schools.summary: Gill: the Jews engaged for themselves, their children, and proselytes, quoting the canon that binds all classes to read the Megillah.
Keil and Delitzsch: they ordained inviolably that they and their seed and all who joined them should keep the two days at their appointed time.
Wesley: the proselytes were included the rather because they too were saved by this deliverance, without which the nation had been extinct.

themes: the proselytes' share in the rescue

schools.summary: Gill, from Aben Ezra: 'every province, every city' is added lest the isolated Jew think himself excused—wherever he is, he is bound.
Keil and Delitzsch render the double guarantee: kept through every generation, never failing nor perishing from their seed.
Henry: God works no wonder merely for a day but for everlasting remembrance (Eccl. 3:14)—remembering Haman's malice, Esther's service, and their own prayers.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'with all authority' as 'with all strength,' to give the letter the force of law, calling it second with reference to Mordecai's letter of v.20; Ellicott makes the first letter the king's (Esther 8:8), so this second is Mordecai's, now confirmed.
Wesley: the former letter (v.20) only recommended, this enjoins, being the act of all the Jews binding their posterity; Clarke: Esther and Mordecai had the king's licence and great authority.
Gill: Esther adds her sanction, perhaps because some had grown backward in the keeping.

debates.question: Which letter is the 'first,' making this the 'second'?

sides.position: this present Esther-and-Mordecai letter is the second; the first is Mordecai's of v.20
the 'second letter' is Mordecai's of v.20; the first is the king's of Esther 8:8

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: copies sent to all 127 provinces, 'words of peace and truth,' appointing the days in their seasons with the matters of fasting and lamentation; Ellicott drops the article—'letters,' not 'the letters.'
Gill: Mordecai sent them, signed in the queen's name and his own.
Wesley: 'peace and truth' means friendship and kindness to the brethren, and sincerity.

Keil and Delitzsch join the fasting and cry to Esther and Mordecai's injunction; Ellicott notes the single verb ('stablish' of v.21) and, though the LXX omits 'the matters of the fastings and their cry,' keeps it, connecting it with the fast of Adar 13.

Wesley traces the 'cry' to the strong supplications of all the Jews when the danger was fresh; Clarke notes no high priest's approbation and no authority beyond Mordecai and Esther, the king having nothing to do with the Jewish religion.
Gill: to confirm the days in their appointed times, the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar.

outliers.note: Stresses that the feast rests on purely Jewish authority—no high priest, no king—since the king had no part in the Jewish religion.

schools.summary: Clarke: Esther's decree was universally received, noting the Vulgate and Targum readings; Wesley takes 'the book' for the Jews' own records of memorable passages.
Gill: the decree of Esther confirmed Purim for all future generations.
Ellicott doubts 'the book' means the Book of Esther itself (an unnatural self-reference), canvassing a book on the festival or, with Rawlinson, the Persian royal chronicles.

debates.question: What is 'the book' in which the decree was written?

sides.position: the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia
the Jews' own records of memorable events
